extracted.intended_audience: postsecondary Title IX coordinators, administrators, decision-makers, hearing officers, and institutional legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts regulatory criteria and procedural standards for conducting Title IX grievance processes at postsecondary institutions, including evidentiary rules (rape-shield, relevance), training, live-hearing requirements, use of technology, and parties' rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on relying on statements of non-cross-examined parties/witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(6)(i) directs a decision-maker not to rely on the statement of a party who has not appeared or submitted to cross-examination and not to draw any inference about responsibility based on a party's absence or refusal to be cross-examined (or refusal to answer other questions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This modification protects respondents exercising Fifth Amendment rights and applies equally to complainants who choose not to appear or testify. Decision-makers are precluded from considering such statements as evidence in their determination of responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-maker must determine relevance of each cross-examination question before answer
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations explicitly state that only relevant questions may be asked, and the decision-maker must determine the relevance of each cross-examination question before a party or witness must answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers are trained to assess relevance, including application of rape-shield protections, and must make contemporaneous determinations of relevance at the live hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-makers must be trained on relevance and rape-shield protections
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(1)(iii) requires decision-makers to be trained on issues of relevance, including specific application of the rape-shield protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training may include information about Fed. R. Evid. 412 Advisory Committee Notes so long as it remains focused on applying the rape-shield protections as formulated in the regulations. Training ensures decision-makers can accurately determine relevance and irrelevance of sexual-history evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rape-shield rule — general exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations deem questions and evidence about a complainant's prior sexual behavior or predisposition to be 'not relevant' (i.e., not admissible) except under two narrow exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors Fed. R. Evid. 412 language and is intended to prevent harassment, slut-shaming, or character/reputation evidence based on sexual history. The regulations clarify that such material is irrelevant across stages unless an exception applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rape-shield exceptions — 'someone other than the respondent' and 'offered to prove consent'
rubrics_metrics.description: Two exceptions permit otherwise excluded sexual-history evidence: (1) if offered to prove that someone other than the respondent committed the alleged misconduct; (2) if the evidence concerns specific sexual behavior between the complainant and respondent and is offered to prove consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scope of the 'prove consent' exception depends in part on the recipient's adopted definition of consent. The first exception requires the respondent to contend another person committed the misconduct; it is narrow and uncommon compared to consent defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient-defined consent determines scope of consent exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations do not define 'consent' and allow recipients flexibility to adopt a definition that reflects values or state law; the recipient's definition of consent will determine the scope of the rape-shield exception referring to 'consent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers will be trained in how to apply the recipient's adopted definition of consent to the rape-shield language. Because of this flexibility, the Department rejects the claim that the exception is unduly broad or favors respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative evidence exchange vs. relevance in reports and hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators must permit exchange of all evidence 'directly related to the allegations' during investigation, but the investigative report must summarize only 'relevant' evidence (excluding sexual-history information deemed 'not relevant'), and decision-makers must objectively evaluate only 'relevant' evidence during the hearing and when reaching a determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exchange of 'directly related' evidence is broader than what is summarized or evaluated for relevance. The rape-shield protections apply at the point of summarizing (investigative report) and at the hearing (decision-maker evaluation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance is sole gatekeeper; no balancing test required
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to impose a balancing test (probative value vs. potential harm/prejudice) for sexual-behavior evidence, because such an open-ended standard is difficult for lay decision-makers to apply; relevance (with the rape-shield exceptions) is the evidentiary gatekeeper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers retain discretion to assign weight or credibility to evidence. The regulations avoid complex balancing tests to keep determinations concrete and administrable by non-lawyers.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement to 'lay a foundation' and hearsay not specifically addressed
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations decline to require respondents to 'lay a foundation' before asking questions or to impose rules excluding questions based on hearsay or speculation; the rulemaker chose relevance as the main gatekeeping standard instead of formal evidentiary foundations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the regulations do not formally adopt hearsay rules, §106.45(b)(6)(i) precludes relying on statements of parties or witnesses who have not been cross-examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual-history evidence about conduct with persons other than respondent excluded from consent exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'offered to prove consent' exception does not admit sexual-history evidence of a complainant's sexual behavior with someone other than the respondent; only sexual behavior between the complainant and the respondent may be considered under that exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents 'slut-shaming' or argument that extensive sexual history with others implies consent with the respondent; admissibility depends on recipient's consent definition and relevance to the specific allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual predisposition deemed irrelevant without exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department uses the phrase 'sexual predisposition' mirroring Fed. R. Evid. 412 and states such evidence is simply irrelevant with no exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aims to foreclose arguments about a complainant's sexual practices or disposition being relevant to credibility or responsibility determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-maker discretion to evaluate weight/credibility; demeanor not sole factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision-makers retain discretion regarding the weight or credibility to assign to particular evidence, and should not judge credibility based solely on demeanor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credibility assessment should consider consistency, plausibility, and reliability in addition to demeanor; reliance solely on observed demeanor or perceived evidence of trauma is cautioned against as inaccurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties' right to advisors and accommodations during hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Final regulations provide both parties the right to be supported and assisted by an advisor of choice (including to conduct cross-examination) and do not preclude recipients from adopting rules (applied equally) governing breaks and conferences with advisors during a hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisors may conduct cross-examination virtually; rules on breaks/conferences must be even-handed between complainants and respondents to ameliorate trauma and support fair participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upon request, recipients must permit cross-examination with parties in separate rooms using technology
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(6)(i) requires recipients, upon any party's request, to permit cross-examination to occur with the parties located in separate rooms using technology that enables participants to see and hear the person answering questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shielding provision acknowledges the intimidating nature of cross-examination and allows the full value of cross-examination while protecting complainants from in-person confrontation. Technology must be reliable and secure; recipients must guard confidentiality and prevent 'live streaming' outside hearing participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire live hearing may be held with parties in separate rooms or virtually upon party request
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations were revised to provide that upon a party's request the entire live hearing (not only cross-examination) must occur with the parties located in separate rooms; recipients, in their discretion, may hold live hearings virtually or permit any participant to appear remotely using technology enabling participants to see and hear each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This balances testing statements for credibility with accommodations for sensitive matters. Recipients may adopt virtual or hybrid models but must ensure technology supports confidentiality and effective participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality obligations constrain technology use
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are obligated under §106.71 to keep confidential the identity of reporters, complainants, respondents, and witnesses except as permitted by FERPA, required by law, or necessary to conduct the proceeding; technology used must not expose testimony to persons outside those participating in the hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must ensure secure platforms and processes so that remote testimony does not inadvertently become public or accessible to others not authorized to attend.

rubrics_metrics.name: No automatic right for witnesses to demand separate-room testimony; recipient discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to grant witnesses the right to demand to testify in a separate room, but revises §106.45(b)(6)(i) to allow a recipient the discretion to permit any participant to appear remotely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witnesses normally are less likely to experience trauma and are not required to testify; for witnesses who claim to have been assaulted, recipients have discretion to permit remote testimony or hold entire hearing virtually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live hearings required at conclusion of investigation (postsecondary institutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations require postsecondary institutions to hold live hearings at the conclusion of an investigation of a formal complaint, ensuring decision-makers hear from parties and witnesses and giving both parties opportunities to present, review, contest, and rebut evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department believes live hearings increase reliability of outcomes and reduce biased decision-making; commenters argued for optional hearings, but the Department maintained the live-hearing requirement while allowing shielding/remote participation options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients should not be compelled via regulations to provide technology grants
rubrics_metrics.description: While the Department recognizes some recipients may incur costs to acquire technology to enable separate rooms or remote participation, the regulations do not provide grant funding and do not address eligibility or purpose of grant funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must bear the costs of implementing technology requirements; the Department notes low-cost solutions are often available and that shielding provisions do not necessarily require capital renovations.
